newsitem.title: UK: PGM dealers sit on fence ahead of Almaz exports.
newsitem.headline: PGM dealers sit on fence ahead of Almaz exports.

text.p: London platinum group metals (PGMs) dealers were preparing to "sit on the fence" for the next few weeks until Russia has begun exporting metal for the first time this year.

The deputy chief executive of Russia's precious metals export agency Almazjuvelirexport (Almaz) confirmed a report on Thursday that deliveries of palladium and platinum to Japan may start at the end of March or the beginning of April.
"It's fully possible at the end of March or the beginning of April," Alexander Kulichkov told Reuters, adding, "it's more possible than not possible."
Russia has not exported PGMs this year after administrative and budgetary problems delayed the start of supply contract talks with Japan.
Japan is the world's leading consumer of palladium and Russia is the world's largest exporter.
"We may see some profit taking on Almaz," one dealer said after palladium had been sold down a couple of dollars under Wednesday's $155.50/$156.50 close.

However others were less certain. "The market is very cynical about it all. Nobody knows who is in charge or who is to be believed. There are no rumours of talks beginning with (Japanese) trade houses," another dealer said.

"Palladium was looking weaker early but it came back up and is being whipped about a bit," the dealer continued. "I would rather sit on the fence. It is all down to how the Russians manage this situation."
Market sources said there was no evidence of Almaz having had talks with the Japanee trade houses yet so any selling in the next few weeks would be into the dealer market.
"If they sell it on to the market (the material) could go everywhere. The Japanese trade houses will be able to buy spot if they want," a senior market analyst said.
"It is impossible to know the volumes involved. To some extent spot selling could substitute for a contract," he added.
The analyst noted, "If they try to make up what they have lost in exports all at once, they will shatter the price."
If that doesn't happen, then there could be some buying to come for palladium, dealers said.
The palladium market is reasonably tight with a one-month lease rate at about 3 percent, but it is not as tight as it was last month.
Russian exports would relieve more pressure as there would be less need for consumers to draw on stocks.
"The Japanese have been working down stocks and the market did tighten up. Russia can maintain market balance or flood it,' the market analyst said.
Russia has always sold some spot material and some on contract. "Selling spot gives them a chance to beat the average price," one palladium market source said.
Almaz said that the start of exports hinged on a resolution awaiting signature by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.
Dealers were less sure it would be as straight forward as that.

"This might be significant for Almaz but how significant is it for the prime minister? He has still to decide who is in charge. He has more problems than just palladium exports, although they must need the dollars," one dealer said.
He added however that once Almaz did start selling, the palladium price could be in trouble.
"As soon as a trader gets an offer from Almaz, he will double it up and sell aggressively. There will be a bit of a collapse," he said.
